title: How someone becomes a saint
hookLine: a life examined, then usually miracles investigated, then a declaration

lines: BOXES OF PAPER ABOUT ONE LIFE.
SOMEONE ARGUES AGAINST HER, ON PURPOSE.
cards: Somewhere in an office in Rome, there are boxes of paper about a woman who died in a small town. Letters she wrote. Interviews with neighbors who knew her.

A doctor's report about a sick child who recovered after people asked her to pray for the child. Someone has read every page. Someone else has argued against her, on purpose, looking for the weak spots.
It might take years, longer than anyone in the town lives. All of it to answer one question carefully.

teach.b: Canonization is the Church's formal declaration that a person is a saint: that they are with God, and can be honored and asked for prayers by the whole Church. First, what it doesn't do.
In Catholic teaching, canonization doesn't make anyone holy. It recognizes a holiness that was already there; the Church is declaring, not creating. Second, how slow it is.
A cause usually begins in the diocese where the person died, when the bishop there agrees to open it.

teach.h: A LIFE EXAMINED FOR HEROIC VIRTUE.
teach.b: Then comes the examination of the life: writings read, witnesses heard, the whole story laid out.
The question is whether this person lived the virtues, faith, hope and love, along with prudence, justice, courage and self-control, to a heroic degree.
Jesus gave a test for that kind of thing in the Sermon on the Mount, in the Douay-Rheims: "By their fruits you shall know them." The investigators are looking for fruit.
Next, usually, comes a miracle: a healing, for instance, that doctors examine and cannot explain, after people asked this person to pray for them.
The Church treats that as a sign that the person is with God. For martyrs the process can differ, but the investigation is still real.

teach.h: BY THEIR FRUITS YOU SHALL KNOW THEM.
teach.b: Through all of it, objections get a hearing: an official's task is to raise them, a role older tradition nicknamed the devil's advocate.
Only at the end does the pope make the declaration, at a Mass, stating formally that this person is a saint.

how: A cause for canonization usually opens in the diocese where the person died, gathers testimony and writings, goes to the Vatican's Dicastery for the Causes of Saints, and, usually after an investigated miracle, ends with the pope declaring the person a saint at a canonization Mass.

adding a book to the Bible's official list
the Church declaring someone a saint

games.q: you're on the team examining a beloved local woman's cause. everyone in town already calls her a saint. what do you do?
o: agree with the town and sign off.
read everything and let someone argue against her.
close the cause to avoid controversy.
games.why: the process is built to test, not to agree: writings read, witnesses heard, objections raised. only then a declaration.

practice: Bring to mind one person you've known whose life bore good fruit: a patience, a kindness, a way they treated people nobody noticed. Don't declare anything about them; just notice the fruit.
If you pray, give thanks for them; if not, let them stay with you for a while.

wordCard.voice: Canonization. The Church's formal declaration, after a long examination, that a person is a saint, to be honored by the whole Church.

orig.note: Latin: holy, saint. a canonization declares that a person is 'sanctus.'

carryVoice: Your line: tested, then declared. The Church declares; it doesn't create. Day nine hundred forty-eight, done.
